newsitem.title: USA: Western U.S electric trade questions natgas impact.
newsitem.headline: Western U.S electric trade questions natgas impact.

text.p: Traders of spot electricity in the western U.S. say natural gas prices do not have as much of a seasonal correlation with electricity prices as the futures market appears to assume.
But the psychological connection between the two markets can often be strong.
Electricity futures on NYMEX have climbed steadily this week, driven in part, according to some futures traders, by weather-related gains in natural gas futures early in the week.
Both NYMEX electricity contracts have delivery points in the western U.S., while the bulk of natural gas futures trade is in the NYMEX Henry Hub contract deliverable in Erath, La.

Before dipping on Thursday, Henry Hub momentum helped propel spot natural gas prices in both the Southwest and Northwest sharply upward, leaving some to attribute strength in electricity to the gas rally.
But later this week, electricity continued to set new highs, while spot gas prices were under some pressure.

"When gas prices were screaming higher earlier this week, the word was that electricity prices had to move up too," said one trader. "But (Thursday) gas craters, electricity keeps moving up, and everyone starts saying gas isn't the fuel-on-margin in the winter. You can't have it both ways."

In the winter off-peak season, coal is considered the fuel-on-margin in the Southwest. In the Northwest, natural gas is now considered the fuel-on-margin during peak demand hours, but hydropower is close behind, sources said.
"There are some constraints on water right now and coal is base-loaded," said another Northwest trade source.

He was referring to "Vernita Bar" requirements on the Columbia River, which are in effect between early October and mid-November. During this period, daytime dam flows must be low enough for them to be maintained until the spring thaw, but high enough so that fish nests do not dry out.

The requirements are believed to be a factor in the Bonneville Power Administration's decision Thursday to refrain from offering surplus spot power, and to offer power only during peak hours on Monday.
Thursday's sharp run-up in both spot and futures markets for electricity was a knee-jerk reaction to BPA's move, despite its likely short-term nature, sources said.
"The market is really top-heavy. We will probably see a big drop before November expires, especially if gas comes down again," said an electricity trader.
NYMEX November electricity contracts expire Monday, while the spot Henry Hub gas contract goes off the board later today.
If, however, BPA stays out of the market, electricity prices will probably be supported, sources said.
"The fact that BPA is out of the market--even for just a day--will drive up the futures prices for the next 18 months," predicted one dealer.
